paper_title: iMFPO: Improving Mean Flow Policy Optimization with Drift-Aware Velocity Alignment for Embodied Control

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Flow-based generative policies offer expressive action modeling for embodied control, yet achieving efficient one-step generation under reward-driven policy optimization remains challenging. In particular, evolving action distributions during online reinforcement learning may introduce inconsistencies between instantaneous-velocity learning and interval-averaged action generation. To address this challenge, we propose iMFPO, a one-step generative policy optimization framework with decoupled velocity learning and drift-aware velocity alignment. A shared interval-conditioned actor supports instantaneous-velocity supervision and interval-averaged action generation. JVP-corrected velocity regression is jointly optimized with reward-driven policy objectives, with action-level guidance from a frozen PPO teacher during training. At inference, iMFPO directly generates actions through interval-averaged velocity prediction, achieving one-step control without iterative flow integration. Across Go2, G1, H1, and Spot, zero-latent evaluation yields mean returns of 35.69, 34.44, 416.23, and 29.86. On Go2, action-generation latency drops from 15.57 ms to 0.41 ms relative to 64-step RFPO. Code: https://github.com/AIGeeksGroup/iMFPO. Website: https://aigeeksgroup.github.io/iMFPO.

Across Go2, G1, H1, and Spot, zero-latent evaluation yields mean returns of 35.69, 34.44, 416.23, and 29.86. On Go2, actiongeneration latency drops from 15.57 ms to 0.41 ms relative to 64-step RFPO. Code & Website. 1. Introduction Recent advances in spatial understanding, video reasoning, and vision-language-action learning have expanded the capabilities of embodied intelligence [8, 9, 11]. However, reliable physical interaction requires expressive control policies with low inference latency. Generative policies offer flexible modeling of complex action distributions. Diffusion models generate actions through iterative denoising [7, 29] and have shown promising results in robotic manipulation and control [2, 26, 31]. Flow matching [18, 19] provides an alternative through continuous velocity fields. Recent flow-based policy optimization methods, including FPO [21], FPO++ [32], and RFPO [10], further improve generative policies through reinforcement learning. Nevertheless, iterative generation introduces substantial inference overhead, limiting its use in real-time robotic control. One-step generative modeling offers promising solution to this limitation. MeanFlow [5] enables direct generation through interval-averaged velocity prediction, while Improved MeanFlow (iMF) [6] reformulates training as instantaneous-velocity regression. Recent robotic methods extend these ideas through velocity constraints, directional alignment, and reinforcement learning [3, 4, 14, 33, 37]. However, integrating one-step velocity learning with online policy optimization remains challenging. MeanFlow-based objectives involve model-dependent velocity predictions and Jacobianvector products (JVPs). Meanwhile, rewarddriven policy updates continuously change the action distribution and its associated velocity targets. This interaction can introduce inconsistencies between instantaneousvelocity supervision and interval-averaged action generation. key challenge is therefore to coordinate velocity learning with policy improvement under evolving rollout distributions. To address this challenge, we propose iMFPO, onestep generative policy optimization framework for embodied control  (Fig. 1)  . Our framework builds on shared interval-conditioned actor that supports two complementary velocity representations. At zero-length intervals, the actor estimates instantaneous velocities for training. Over the full interval, it predicts the average velocity required for direct noise-to-action generation. This design connects local velocity supervision with one-step action prediction without introducing separate networks. It also allows both learning objectives to operate within unified policy representation. We further introduce drift-aware velocity alignment to keep instantaneous-velocity supervision, interval-averaged generation, and reward-driven updates consistent as the rollout distribution drifts. Specifically, JVP-corrected velocity regression provides supervision for the shared velocity field, while loss-induced policy surrogate aligns that field with reward feedback from online rollouts. frozen PPO teacher supplies additional action-level guidance during training. These components jointly align the actors velocity predictions under evolving policy distributions. At inference, the learned policy generates actions with single network evaluation, without iterative flow integration or teacher guidance. Experiments across four robotic embodiments demonstrate competitive control performance with substantially reduced inference latency. The main contributions are summarized as follows: We propose iMFPO, one-step MeanFlow policy optimization framework that decouples instantaneousvelocity learning from interval-averaged action generation through shared interval-conditioned actor. We introduce drift-aware velocity alignment, which couples JVP-corrected iMF regression with velocitybased policy ratio so that reward updates reshape the same interval-conditioned field used for one-step generation under evolving rollouts. We demonstrate competitive one-step control performance across four robotic embodiments, achieving mean returns of 35.69, 34.44, 416.23, and 29.86 on Go2, G1, H1, and Spot, respectively. On Go2, iMFPO reduces action-generation latency from 15.57 ms to 0.41 ms compared with 64-step RFPO, with additional real-world locomotion demonstrations. 2. Related Work Generative policies for robot control. Generative policies have emerged as expressive alternatives to conventional unimodal action distributions, enabling the modeling of complex and multimodal robot behaviors. Diffusion Policy [2] demonstrates the effectiveness of diffusion models for visuomotor control, while Diffusion Q-Learning [31] and Diffusion Policy Policy Optimization (DPPO) [26] extend diffusion-based policies to reinforcement learning (RL). Alternatively, flow matching [18] and rectified flow [19] formulate generation through continuous velocity fields, offering efficient transport-based generative modeling. Recent approaches, including consistency models [30], FlowPolicy [35], and Flow Q-Learning [25], further explore efficient action generation. For language-guided legged navigation, NaVILA [1] combines VILA-based visual-language model [17] with locomotion policy through metric midlevel commands. Real-time robotic control places action quality, optimization efficiency, and inference latency under shared deployment constraint. Legged locomotion and visual navigation. Early sim-to-real studies demonstrated learned dynamic motor skills [12] and proprioceptive locomotion over challenging terrain [16]. Massively parallel reinforcement learning enables rapid training of quadrupedal locomotion policies [27], while RMA [15] adapts simulated policy online to changing terrain and robot dynamics. Rapid Locomotion [20] studies high-speed velocity tracking and transfer to physical quadruped, and perceptive locomotion [22] uses exteroceptive sensing to traverse challenging terrain. For vision-and-language navigation, NaVid [34] predicts the next action from an instruction and video stream. Our experiments focus on one-step low-level action generation under velocity commands, including commands issued by NaVILA. Reinforcement learning for flow policies. Building upon proximal policy optimization (PPO) [28], recent studies have investigated RL optimization of flow-based policies. ReinFlow [36] introduces stochastic transitions into flow trajectories to enable likelihood-based online policy optimization. Flow Policy Optimization (FPO) [21] instead constructs policy optimization surrogate using conditional flow-matching losses, avoiding explicit likelihood computation. FPO++ [32] further improves optimization stability through per-sample importance ratios and an asymmetric trust region. To address performance degradation under coarse numerical integration, Rectified Flow Policy Optimization [10] employs reward-aware online reflow and teacher-guided supervision for reliable few-step execution. Refinement-Based Flow Policy Optimization [24] alternatively combines Q-guided action refinement with self-target flow matching to improve the learned action distribution. Our setting focuses on learning one-step velocity representation during reward-driven policy updates. MeanFlow and one-step policy optimization. MeanFlow [5] enables one-step generation by directly predicting interval-averaged velocities, eliminating the need Improved MeanFlow for (iMF) [6] reformulates its self-dependent training objective as instantaneous-velocity regression, while further analysis [13] investigates the relationship between instantaneous and average velocities. For robotic control, Mean Velocity Policy (MVP) introduces instantaneous- [33] velocity boundary constraints, whereas One-step MeanFlow Policy (OMP) [4] employs directional velocity alignment and efficient Jacobianvector product approximation. Recent studies have also extended MeanFlow to RL. Mean Flow Policy Optimization (MFPO) [3] develops maximum-entropy policy optimization framework, while Dispersive MeanFlow Policy Optimization (DMPO) [37] and Score-Based One-step MeanFlow Policy Optimization (SOM) [14] incorporate dispersive regularization and Q-guided velocity targets, respectively. One-Step Flow Q-Learning [23] further explores average-velocity representations for offline RL. Our work studies the interaction between instantaneous-velocity supervision, intervalaveraged action generation, and reward-driven policy updates within shared one-step actor. iterative ODE integration. 3. Method 3.1. Overview As illustrated in Fig. 2, we present iMFPO, one-step generative policy optimization framework that connects local velocity learning with finite-interval action generation through shared actor. Decoupled velocity learning assigns complementary roles to instantaneous and intervalaveraged velocities. Drift-aware velocity alignment couples iMF velocity regression with reward-driven updates on the shared interval-conditioned field under evolving rollout distributions. During training, auxiliary action-level guidance further regularizes the shared velocity field, promoting stable one-step action generation. The resulting actor produces actions in single forward pass without iterative flow integration. 3.2. Drift-Aware Velocity Alignment Online policy improvement changes the action distribution between rollout iterations, so the actions and velocity targets used to train uθ evolve with the policy. We align reward-driven updates with velocity learning on the current rollout distribution through shared surrogate. Instead of introducing separate action likelihood, we construct the policy ratio from changes in the iMF residual on stored interval-conditioned tuples. This design keeps reward updates inside the same velocity field that produces one-step actions at deployment, which is the core of drift-aware velocity alignment. In particular, policy improvement and iMF regression share the stored (o, a, ϵ, r, t) tuples collected online, so distribution shift is handled without switching the deployed generator. Because each tuple stores the interval endpoints (r, t) used during collection, the same surrogate can act on instantaneous endpoints and longer chords without changing the actor architecture. As result, instantaneous supervision through JVPiMF and full-interval generation remain coupled under one trustregion signal while the rollout distribution drifts. This asymmetric treatment limits large destructive updates while still allowing informative positive-advantage steps to reshape uθ. Tab. 1 summarizes returns across four embodiments under matched evaluation protocol. Under zero-latent initialization, iMFPO obtains 35.69, 34.44, 416.23, and 29.86 on Go2, G1, H1, and Spot with single network evaluation. These scores are comparable to, or slightly above, the corresponding 64-NFE RFPO baselines (35.58, 32.55, 416.06, and 28.19). This indicates that policy trained for fullinterval MeanFlow prediction can match strong multistep flow optimizer at test time with one network evaluation. The cross-embodiment consistency further indicates that the shared one-step actor transfers across quadruped and humanoid morphologies under the same evaluation protocol. Reducing FPO++ from 64 NFEs to 1 NFE causes large degradations on every robot (for example, Go2 falls from 18.56 to 185.70). This pattern indicates that multistep solver trained for fine numerical integration becomes unreliable when forced to act with single coarse step. iMFPO instead optimizes the deployed map in Eq. (12) during training, so reward updates reshape the same intervalconditioned field used at inference. Aligning the training objective with the inference map therefore explains why one-step deployment remains competitive with 64NFE RFPO. Under random latents, iMFPO remains stable on Go2 (35.34), G1 (30.79), H1 (406.77), and Spot (30.15). 1-NFE RFPO stays close to its 64-NFE score on Go2 and Spot, but drops sharply on G1 from 33.59 (Zero) to 17.71 (Random). Tab. 3 isolates design choices that implement decoupled velocity learning on Go2. Removing JVPiMF lowers zeroand random-latent returns from 35.69 and 35.34 to 29.21 and 26.24. The larger randomlatent drop indicates that localinterval consistency matters more when the initial latent varies, supporting Contribution 1 and the JVP correction in Eq. (6). This small change indicates that matching the deployed interval (r, t) = (0, 1) already captures most of the one-step objective, while random-r sampling provides an additional refinement. Removing the interval iMF regression term yields 21.00 and 18.91, which indicates that finite-interval velocity learning is essential for stable one-step control under the same ρF+KD recipe. At matched σ = 0 starting points, both methods are competitive, so later divergence is attributable to increasing noise scale. As σ increases, 1-NFE RFPO degrades sharply, whereas ρF-trained iMFPO stays nearly flat. This indicates that drift-aware velocity alignment keeps moderate noise-endpoint perturbations inside transport optimized end-to-end by ρF and iMF. Fig. 4 visualizes the action distributions generated by iMFPO on Go2. For fixed observation, we sample multiple noise inputs and visualize the marginal densities of all twelve action dimensions. The distributions gradually concentrate from noise to actions, with orange curves indicating the mean trajectories. The horizontal axis denotes generation progress = 1 t, from noise (s = 0) to actions (s = 1). Figure 6. Go2 navigation and locomotion keyframes. Real-world navigation sequences (top) and real/simulated locomotion examples (bottom). Velocity tracking. We replay three recorded Go2 velocitycommand trajectories in Isaac Lab using the 1-NFE iMFPO controller at 50 Hz. The trajectories cover forward, lateral, and turning motions, each lasting approximately 19 20 seconds. All simulated rollouts complete without falls. The mean absolute tracking errors range from 0.014 to 0.145 m/s longitudinally and from 0.025 to 0.093 m/s laterally. Fig. 5 shows the velocity responses and planar trajectories. The results demonstrate stable velocity tracking under different motion commands. Real-world demonstrations. Fig. 6 presents real-world Go2 navigation sequences and real/simulation locomotion comparisons. The results illustrate the deployment of the 1NFE controller on physical robot and its integration with high-level navigation commands. MuJoCo scene with an obstacle between the robot and the target. scripted mid-level command sequence brings the robot within 0.52 of the chair without fall. NaVILAdriven rollouts and the remaining instructions are shown in Figs. 1 and 6. These results illustrate the integration of language-guided navigation with one-step locomotion control. 5. Limitations Our quantitative evaluation focuses on flat velocity tracking in simulation, without systematic terrain or disturbance stress tests. Reported returns use selected checkpoints, and real-robot results are qualitative rather than full tracking or navigation success rates. 4.5. Language-Guided Control 6. Conclusion We connect NaVILA [1] to the frozen Go2 iMFPO locomotion controller. Given language instruction, NaVILA generates mid-level navigation commands, which are converted into planar velocity targets and executed by the 1-NFE controller. We consider three spatial instructions: Go near the chair, Go between the trash can and the chair, and Go near the door. Figs. 1 and 6 show the corresponding execution sequences. For the chair instruction, we evaluate We presented iMFPO, one-step generative policy optimization framework for embodied control. shared actor decouples instantaneous-velocity learning from intervalaveraged action generation, and drift-aware velocity alignment couples iMF regression with reward-driven updates under evolving rollouts. Across four embodiments, iMFPO supports competitive one-step control. On Go2, it reaches 35.69 return while reducing action-generation latency from 15.57 ms to 0.41 ms versus 64-step RFPO. Command replay and language-guided control further illustrate the controller in extended pipelines. Future work will study broader alignment objectives and real-world generalization.

sections.title: Supplementary Material
sections.content: A. Additional Experimental Details A.1. Training Configurations We provide additional implementation details for the locomotion experiments across Go2, G1, H1, and Spot. All embodiments share the same interval-conditioned policy representation and one-step action generation formulation, while their policy optimization objectives follow the corresponding exploration configurations. The actor and critic are implemented as multilayer perceptrons with ELU activations. The actor contains three hidden layers of 256 units, while the critic uses three hidden layers of 768 units. The shared optimization hyperparameters are summarized in Tab. S1. Table S1. Shared training configurations. Setting Optimizer Learning rate Discount factor γ GAE parameter λ Optimization epochs Mini-batches Rollout horizon (steps) Trust-region bound δ Actor architecture Critic architecture Activation Interval sampling Boundary probability pb Value AdamW 1 104 0.99 0.95 16 4 24 0.05 [256, 256, 256] [768, 768, 768] ELU U(0, t) 0.25 Tab. S2 summarizes the embodiment-specific environment configurations. The action dimensionality follows the corresponding robot control interfaces. Table S2. Robot-specific configurations. Robot Parallel environments Action dimension Go2 G1 (29-DoF) H1 Spot 4096 2048 4096 4096 12 29 19 12 The Go2 training schedule consists of an initial optimization stage followed by checkpoint-based refinement. The initial stage runs for 1,500 iterations with teachermatching coefficient of 0.1. The subsequent refinement stage runs for 1,001 iterations, increasing the coefficient to 0.2. The Spot training curve reports the initial 1,500iteration stage. A.2. Policy Optimization and Inference Interval-conditioned training. At each optimization iteration, an on-policy batch is collected using the current actor. Given an action and Gaussian noise ϵ, an intermediate state is constructed as zt = (1 t)a + tϵ. (13) The interval endpoint is sampled according to U(0, t), with the boundary case = selected with probability pb = 0.25. Both interval-averaged and instantaneous velocity predictions are obtained from the same actor. Embodiment-specific policy updates. The policy optimization follows the exploration configuration of each embodiment. For Go2, the iMF regression error contributes to the loss-induced policy ratio used for reward-driven policy improvement. For G1, H1, and Spot, diagonal Gaussian exploration policy is used, with the one-step actor prediction serving as its mean. An additional advantage-weighted iMF regression objective supervises the velocity representation using positive-advantage samples. Teacher-guided training. frozen PPO teacher provides action-level supervision through teacher-matching objective. The teacher parameters remain fixed throughout student optimization. This supervision is applied only during training and does not introduce additional inference-time computation. Deployment. At deployment, the actor is evaluated over the full interval (r, t) = (0, 1): aθ(o, ϵ) = ϵ uθ(o, ϵ, 0, 1). (14) Only the shared actor is retained. The critic, frozen teacher, velocity-regression objective, and JVP computation are discarded. Consequently, each action is generated using single network evaluation, without iterative flow integration. B. Training Dynamics B.1. Go2 Training Dynamics Fig. S1 presents the complete training trajectory of iMFPO on Go2. The initial optimization stage progressively improves the mean episode reward, although noticeable fluctuations occur throughout online training. At the transition to checkpoint-based refinement, the teacher-matching coefficient is increased from 0.1 to 0.2. The reward subsequently Figure S1. Training dynamics of iMFPO on Go2. (a) Mean episode reward during the initial optimization and refinement stages. The dashed line marks the transition at 1,500 iterations, where the teacher-matching coefficient increases from 0.1 to 0.2. (b) Corresponding teacher-matching and value losses. Figure S2. Training dynamics of iMFPO on Spot. (a) Mean episode reward during the initial training stage. (b) Corresponding teachermatching and value losses. recovers and approaches approximately 35 toward the end of training. The teacher-matching and value losses generally decrease during optimization, with transient peaks at several update intervals. These curves provide complementary diagnostics of the interaction between policy optimization and auxiliary supervision. B.2. Spot Training Dynamics Fig. S2 shows the training trajectory on Spot during the initial optimization stage. The mean episode reward gradually increases and reaches approximately 30. Although several performance drops occur during training, the reward subsequently recovers. The teacher-matching and value losses exhibit corresponding transient fluctuations before decreasing toward smaller values. Together, the Go2 and Spot curves provide additional training diagnostics across two different robotic embodiments, complementing the final evaluation results reported in the main paper. C. Additional Qualitative Results C.1. Cross-Embodiment Locomotion Visualizations Figs. S3S5 provide additional qualitative visualizations of simulated locomotion rollouts across Go2, Spot, G1, and H1. The figures present representative snapshots of policy execution at different timestamps, illustrating locomotion behaviors across robotic embodiments with distinct morphologies and action spaces. These visualizations complement the quantitative results reported in the main paper by providing qualitative observations of the learned one-step generative policies. Figure S3. Cross-embodiment locomotion visualization (I). Representative simulation rollout frames of Go2, Spot, G1, and H1 under the learned one-step generative policies. Figure S4. Cross-embodiment locomotion visualization (II). Additional simulation rollout frames illustrating policy execution across the four robotic embodiments. Figure S5. Cross-embodiment locomotion visualization (III). Representative simulation snapshots providing further qualitative visualizations of the learned locomotion policies.
